title: Virtual memory: why every process thinks it owns the machine

questions.question: There is one memory chip in the phone, and every running app is in it. What keeps one app's memory out of another's reach?
options: Each app is given its own region and stays inside it
Android checks every read against the app's permissions
Each process has its own table of addresses, with no entry for anyone else's memory
Apps are encrypted separately in memory
questions.explanation: There is no guard watching each access, and nothing would stop a stray pointer from leaving a region. The separation is that another app's memory has no address in your process at all.

questions.question: Your code reads an object at a virtual address. What happens between that instruction and the memory chip?
options: The kernel intercepts the read and performs it on your behalf
The MMU translates the address using your process's page table
The address is used directly, because virtual addresses are physical on mobile devices
The runtime looks the object up in a table it maintains
questions.explanation: The translation is done by hardware on every access, which is the only way it can be fast enough to happen millions of times a second. The kernel's job is writing the table, not performing the reads.

questions.question: A process list shows your app with a VSZ of 14 GB on a phone that has 8 GB of memory. What is wrong?
options: The process is leaking memory badly
The tool is reporting kilobytes as gigabytes
Nothing. VSZ counts address space, which is not memory
The app has memory swapped out to storage
questions.explanation: Addresses are invented, so reserving a lot of them costs nothing. The number worth watching is the resident one, which counts pages actually present in physical memory.

questions.question: Your app throws OutOfMemoryError while the device still has plenty of free memory. How can both be true?
options: The runtime applies a heap cap per app, and your app crossed it
The free memory is reserved for the system and unavailable to apps
The allocation was larger than a single page, which is not allowed
The garbage collector had not run yet, so the memory was not really free
questions.explanation: The cap exists so that one app cannot exhaust the device and take everything else down with it. The device having memory left is the point, not a contradiction.

questions.question: A teammate proposes passing a raw memory address from your app to another app so it can read your data directly. Why will that never work?
options: The address would need to be sent over Binder, which strips pointers
The other process has a different page table, so that number means something else there, or nothing
Android blocks pointer sharing for security reasons
It would work, but only if both apps are signed by the same key
questions.explanation: A virtual address is only meaningful inside the process whose page table defines it. Sharing memory between processes has to be arranged by the kernel, which maps the same physical pages into both address spaces.

questions.question: Why is a stack trace address from one crash report useless when compared with an address from another device's report?
options: Crash reporters obfuscate addresses before uploading them
Addresses change when the app is recompiled
Each process has its own address space, so the same number means nothing across processes
Addresses are only valid while the process is running
questions.explanation: Two processes can hold entirely unrelated data at the same virtual address, so the raw number carries no meaning outside the process that produced it. This is why symbolication maps addresses back to code rather than comparing them.
